Amid Nepal’s devastating floods, a heartbreaking video of a little boy carrying his younger sister has left social media in tears. With scratches visible on their faces, the young boy reportedly searches for their parents while holding tightly onto his little sister. He is just a child himself, yet in a moment of unimaginable disaster, he appears to be protecting the one person he still has. The powerful visuals have reminded many people of Grave of the Fireflies, the heartbreaking story of siblings Seita and Setsuko struggling to survive amid the de*struction of war. But this is not a movie. These are real children, facing a real disaster, searching for the people they love. Sometimes, the most painful images are the ones that need no words. More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

#tragedia  información  @laantenaoficial  —— #atencion #26Ago Nepal busca a cientos de desaparecidos tras una riada Al menos 55 personas murieron y 403 permanecen desaparecidas este miércoles después de que una riada repentina golpeara varias localidades cerca de la frontera con el Tíbet (China), según confirmaron las autoridades. El portavoz de la Policía de Nepal en la provincia de Bagmati, Rajendra Prasad Dhamala, elevó a 55 las personas fallecidas en el desastre que golpeó pueblos, mercados, carreteras y obras hidroeléctricas a primera hora de la mañana. Al mismo tiempo, la Junta de Turismo de Nepal aseguró que 403 personas, entre ellas 341 extranjeras, permanecen desaparecidas. Dos de ellas son de nacionalidad española, según las fuentes. El portavoz del Ejército de Nepal, Rajaram Basnet, declaró a EFE que al menos 29 personas habían sido rescatadas tras el desbordamiento del río Bhote Koshi. Basnet señaló que seis helicópteros del Ejército y otros ocho operados por empresas privadas fueron desplegados para las labores de búsqueda y rescate. “Es difícil evaluar los daños en este momento, pero es posible que tanto los daños como el número de víctimas sean considerables”, afirmó. La riada golpeó a primera hora del miércoles el distrito de Rasuwa, donde afectó pueblos, mercados, carreteras y obras hidroeléctricas e interrumpió el tránsito por una de las principales rutas terrestres entre Nepal y el Tíbet. La masa de agua llegó hacia las 9:15 hora local (3:30 GMT) al río Bhote Koshi desde la zona tibetana y golpeó con especial fuerza Timure, Rasuwagadhi y Syabrubesi, según fuentes oficiales. Las autoridades movilizaron a los cuerpos de seguridad y equipos de emergencia mientras trataban de determinar el alcance de los daños y localizar a las personas que permanecían sin contacto. Cada año, miles de personas viajan al monte Kailash y al lago Mansarovar, en el Tíbet, durante una peregrinación considerada sagrada por hindúes, budistas y jainistas. Nepal atribuye a un terremoto el origen de la riada El ministro de Asuntos Exteriores de Nepal, Shishir Khanal, afirmó este miércoles que la repentina riada que ha arrasado varias localidades  #nepal #tibet

Recalling that she had voted for the government with the hope that things would improve, she said she is now deeply disappointed that her missing husband has not been properly searched for. Nepal Flood and Major Health Risks On August 26, 2026, a massive flash flood swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system after a sudden surge of water, ice, rock, and mud from the Himalayan border region. The disaster destroyed communities, roads, bridges, homes, water systems, and hydropower facilities. As of September 4, more than 1,250 people had been reported dead and over 4,200 were still missing, while thousands of people had been displaced from their homes. The destruction has turned the flood from an immediate natural disaster into a serious public-health crisis. (Reuters) One of the biggest health concerns is unsafe drinking water. Flooding damaged water-supply and sanitation systems, which can allow sewage, waste, and other contamination to enter water used for drinking and cooking. UNICEF reports that at least 22,000 children urgently need clean water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance. This creates a greater risk of diarrheal and other waterborne illnesses, especially among young children. (UNICEF) Another major concern is the spread of infectious disease in crowded shelters and temporary housing. Many displaced families are staying together in holding centers or with other households, making respiratory infections easier to spread. Standing water and disrupted sanitation may also increase the risk of mosquito- and other vector-borne diseases. WHO is additionally concerned about contaminated food, infected wounds, injuries caused by debris, and shortages of essential medical care. (World Health Organization) The flood has also damaged Nepal’s ability to provide healthcare. WHO reports that three health posts were completely damaged, one hospital was partially damaged, and access to two other hospitals was affected. This means people may struggle to receive emergency treatment as well as regular care such as medications, maternal care, treatment for chronic diseases, and other essential health services. (World Health Organization) Finally, survivors may face important mental-health effects, including grief, trauma, fear, and stress after losing relatives, homes, or livelihoods. Nepal’s immediate challenge is therefore not only rescuing survivors but also providing clean water, sanitation, food, shelter, medical treatment, disease monitoring, and functioning healthcare services. If these needs are addressed quickly, many illnesses and additional deaths after the flood can be prevented. (World Health Organization) #nepal #floods #nepaltibet #safety
